job_heading: The Job: What We Found, What We Did
job_lead: A chimney that was worth saving. The detail photos are from the same chimney after the work.

found.text: A fieldstone chimney on an older home, and the two problems stone chimneys almost always have. The joints between the irregular stones — far more joint area than a brick chimney — had washed out and were taking in water. And the top of the chimney, the part that takes every freeze-thaw cycle head-on, had deteriorated past the point where repointing alone would hold.

Tearing it down and rebuilding in brick would have been the easy quote. It would also have thrown away the stone that makes the house what it is. The job was to preserve the stone where it was sound and rebuild in concrete only where the chimney was actually failing.

steps.title: Inspection and photos
steps.text: The chimney was checked from the roof and the flue checked from above. The homeowner got the photos and a written price for the restoration before anything started.

steps.title: Stone joints repointed
steps.text: The loose, washed-out mortar was raked out between the stones and the joints packed with fresh mortar — worked into the irregular gaps and tooled, so the stone face stays exposed and the water path is closed.

steps.title: The top rebuilt in concrete
steps.text: The failing upper section was encased in a new concrete coat and finished with a crown around the flue. Concrete here does what the weathered stone top could no longer do: take the weather and shed water away from the chimney.

steps.title: Stainless steel cap fitted
steps.text: A stainless cap with mesh screen was fitted over the flue. It keeps rain and snow out of the flue, keeps birds and animals out, and will not rust.

steps.title: Roofline sealed, site cleared
steps.text: The flashing where the chimney meets the roof was sealed, the roof cleared, and the finished chimney photographed for the homeowner.

why_heading: Why Restore A Stone Chimney Instead Of Replacing It?
why_lead: Stone is the hardest part of an old house to replace. Treat the stone and the top differently, and the chimney gets another long life.

pillars.title: The stone is irreplaceable
pillars.text: Fieldstone chimneys were built from what was on the land. Repointing keeps the original stone and the look of the house; a brick rebuild never quite does.

pillars.title: Concrete where the weather hits
pillars.text: The top of a chimney takes the worst of rain, snow and freeze-thaw. A solid concrete top and crown shed water instead of absorbing it.

pillars.title: Capped and screened
pillars.text: An open flue takes in rain, snow, leaves and animals. A stainless cap closes it off and never needs replacing for rust.

faq.q: Why rebuild the top in concrete rather than in stone?
faq.a: The top of a chimney gets the most weather and the least protection. Where the stone top has deteriorated, a concrete top with a proper crown is the durable fix: it is solid, it sheds water, and it protects the stone below it. The stone that was still sound was repointed and kept exposed.

faq.q: Does repointing stone work differently from brick?
faq.a: Yes. Stone joints are irregular and much wider, so there is more joint to rake out and fill, and the mortar has to be worked into the gaps around each stone rather than along a straight line. It takes longer than brick, and it is the reason washed-out joints are so common on stone chimneys.

Galvanized caps rust and stain the masonry below them within a few years. A stainless cap does not, so it is the last cap the chimney should need. The mesh keeps birds and animals out; the lid keeps rain and snow out of the flue.

faq.q: Can every old chimney be restored, or do some have to come down?
faq.a: Most can be restored, and the free inspection tells you which yours is. A chimney that is leaning, with stone or brick loose through the whole structure, may need a partial or full rebuild. We photograph what we find and price the options in writing.

faq.q: Do you work on stone chimneys across the GTA?
faq.a: Yes — Toronto and the whole GTA, from Etobicoke to Scarborough and north through Vaughan, Richmond Hill and Markham. See where we work.
